Kuder-Richardson Formula 20 (KR-20) With a Confidence Interval

Source: R/reliability_kr20.R
reliability_kr20.Rd

Estimates Kuder-Richardson formula 20 (Kuder & Richardson, 1937) for a homogeneous composite scored on dichotomous (0/1) items, and returns a confidence interval for the population coefficient.

Usage

reliability_kr20(
  data,
  ci_method = c("feldt", "bonett", "fisher", "hakstian_whalen", "ml", "ml_logistic",
    "adf", "adf_logistic", "bootstrap_se", "bootstrap_se_logistic", "percentile", "bca",
    "none"),
  conf_level = 0.95,
  B = 10000,
  seed = NULL,
  ncpus = 1L,
  progress = NULL
)

Arguments

data

A numeric matrix or data frame of 0/1 item scores (rows are respondents, columns are items). Rows with any missing values are listwise-deleted. Non-binary values trigger an error, and so do fewer than two complete rows, from which no variance can be computed. A column that is not numeric, and an item that takes one value in every complete row (one no respondent passes, or every respondent does), are refused by name: such an item adds a constant to the total score, whose reliability it leaves as it is, while KR-20 would count it among the \(J\) items, at \(J(J-2)/(J-1)^2\) times the KR-20 of the other items, the coefficient of the same total. So is a total score that takes one value in every complete row (on two rows, as many items passed in one row as in the other), whose reliability is not defined. For incomplete data, reliability_alpha with missing = "fiml" computes the same coefficient (alpha of 0/1 items is KR-20) from the incomplete rows as well. SPSS user-defined missing values, which haven::read_sav(user_na = TRUE) keeps as values of a haven_labelled_spss column, are missing, as SPSS treats them.

ci_method

Method for constructing the confidence interval; see reliability_alpha for the full list. Defaults to "feldt".

conf_level

Confidence level for the interval (1 - Type I error rate). Defaults to 0.95.

B

Number of bootstrap replications when a bootstrap method is selected, a single whole number. Defaults to 10000. The fewest accepted depends on the interval method and the level: at the default conf_level, 400 for "percentile" (10 replications beyond each limit), 2000 for "bca" (50 beyond each nominal limit, because the adjusted limits sit farther into the tails), and 100 for "bootstrap_se" and "bootstrap_se_logistic" (a standard deviation of the replications); at 0.99 the first two are 2000 and 10000. A smaller B is refused before anything is computed (class dmar_count_invalid). The count is held to the number requested. Replications set aside afterward are counted and reported in a warning of class dmar_bootstrap_replications_dropped, which names the function and says to request more when those that return a value are fewer than the number required; when fewer than half of the B replications return a value, the interval is withheld (limits and bootstrap standard error NA) under a warning of class dmar_bootstrap_insufficient. See dmar_bootstrap, which also describes options(dmar.bootstrap_exploratory = TRUE) for a first look with a smaller B.

seed

Random number seed used for bootstrap reproducibility. Defaults to NULL, under which the resamples are drawn from, and advance, the current random number stream; supply an integer for a reproducible interval, which is set for the call only, the caller's random number state being restored when it returns.

ncpus

The number of processes over which the bootstrap replications are spread. The default 1 runs them in this R session; a larger number uses forked workers (boot's parallel = "multicore") or, on Windows, which cannot fork, a socket cluster ("snow"), whose workers load the installed DMAR. boot draws every resample before any replication runs, so a given seed returns the same interval, counts, and replicates whatever ncpus is. A session that forks workers and also starts background processes through callr or processx needs the environment variable PROCESSX_NOTIFY_OLD_SIGCHLD set before processx is loaded (see sem_exact_fit_bootstrap). Ignored unless a bootstrap method is selected.

progress

NULL (the default), or a function of two arguments that the bootstrap calls as it runs, so that an application can show how far a long bootstrap has gone and let its user stop it (a Shiny app, for example). It is called as progress(done, total), with the number of replications attempted so far and B: after each replication when ncpus = 1, and with more processes after each block of replications they complete together, about a fiftieth of B (ncpus * ceiling(B / (50 * ncpus)) replications, the last block possibly fewer), so that done advances by the block. A BCa interval takes its acceleration from a regression on the resampling frequencies when at least as many replications return a value as there are cases, and from the jackknife, one leave-one-out refit per case, when fewer do or when that regression fails or gives influence values that are not all finite; the jackknife runs at most once in a call, and not at all when no interval is formed or every returned replicate has the same value. While it runs, the callback is called again after each refit (with more processes, after each block of ncpus * ceiling(n / (50 * ncpus)) refits, n the number of cases resampled), with done and total both B, so it can be called more than B times, and done equal to total does not mean that the bootstrap has finished. If the callback returns FALSE, the bootstrap stops before the next replication or block with an error of class dmar_bootstrap_cancelled, whose elements done and total say how far it got (see dmar_metadata); any other value is ignored. An error inside the callback stops the call with an error of class dmar_progress_error, whose message names the callback and which carries done, total, and, as parent, the callback's own condition with its class intact, so that an application can tell a failing callback from a failing analysis. The callback runs outside the random number stream, so a given seed returns the same result with or without it, and a callback that draws random numbers leaves the caller's stream as it found it. With NULL nothing is called. Ignored unless a bootstrap method is selected.

Value

A data.frame with columns term and value and rows "estimate" (sample KR-20), "se" (standard error on the coefficient scale, NA for methods that do not produce one; for the transformation-based intervals "fisher", "bonett", and "hakstian_whalen" it is the delta method back-transform of the transformation-scale standard error), "se_transformed" (only for those transformation-based intervals: the standard error on the transformation scale, with the scale named in the attribute se_transform_scale: "fisher_z", "log(1-alpha)", or "cube_root"), "ci_lower" and "ci_upper" (each clamped into [0, 1], so the limits stay in order), "conf_level", "N" (effective sample size after listwise deletion), "N_complete" (the complete cases; equal to "N" here, and carried so the whole reliability family returns one shape), and "n_items" (number of items). Attributes coefficient ("kr20") and ci_method record the computation; bootstrap calls also record B, the replication counts in the bootstrap attribute (see reliability_alpha; KR-20 fits no model, so no replication is improper), and the number of replications the interval uses in the attribute B_used, with n_dropped, B_required, and bootstrap_status (see dmar_bootstrap).

Details

Kuder and Richardson's (1937) formula 20 for a \(J\)-item composite of binary items is $$KR_{20} = \frac{J}{J-1}\left(1 - \frac{\sum_{j} p_{j} q_{j}}{s_{Y}^{2}}\right),$$ where \(p_{j}\) is the proportion of respondents endorsing item j (i.e., scoring 1), \(q_{j} = 1 - p_{j}\), and \(s_{Y}^{2}\) is the variance of the composite score. For dichotomous items \(p_{j} q_{j}\) is the item variance, so KR-20 is algebraically identical to coefficient \(\alpha\) (Guttman, 1945; Cronbach, 1951) computed from the item covariance matrix. KR-20 predates coefficient \(\alpha\) by 14 years and Feldt's (1965) F-distribution interval was derived specifically for the sampling distribution of KR-20.

Because KR-20 is a special case of coefficient \(\alpha\) (Guttman, 1945; Cronbach, 1951), the same considerations apply: KR-20 equals the population reliability of the composite under essential \(\tau\)-equivalence (i.e., equal factor loadings) and serves as a lower bound otherwise. For dichotomous items see also reliability_omega_categorical (categorical omega), which treats the items via a probit-link single-factor model and does not assume equal loadings.

KR-20, like \(\alpha\), is at most one but can fall below zero, when the item covariances are negative on balance; on dichotomous items that can arise when an item is scored in the opposite direction to the others (a reversed key). A reliability coefficient cannot be negative, so a negative estimate is returned as computed with a warning that says so, and each confidence limit is clamped into [0, 1]; the interval around an estimate far enough below zero is then [0, 0], which says that the data support no positive reliability for the items as keyed.

Available confidence interval methods (set via ci_method) are the same as for reliability_alpha; see that function's Details for full descriptions. The default for KR-20 is "feldt", the F-distribution interval originally developed for KR-20.

From two complete rows KR-20 is computed with Feldt's interval, which is defined for any N of at least 2 (every item must differ between the two rows, since an item they answer alike does not vary, and the two totals must differ, since a total that does not vary has no reliability). Feldt's F reference is exact under multivariate normality and parallel items, which 0/1 items cannot meet, and for them it is the approximation Feldt (1965) derived. The intervals that are not defined there ("bonett", "fisher", "ml", "adf", their _logistic variants, and the bootstrap) are refused, as reliability_alpha explains, and "hakstian_whalen", which is defined, has an upper limit of one there whatever the data, at any confidence level above about .90.

The menu also includes the nonparametric bootstrap intervals "percentile", "bca", "bootstrap_se", and "bootstrap_se_logistic", which resample the rows of data with replacement B times and recompute KR-20 on each replication (Efron & Tibshirani, 1993). They are worth the cost when the closed forms are least trustworthy, which for dichotomous items means highly unbalanced item difficulties or a sample size too small for the normal-theory derivations behind "feldt" and "bonett". No bootstrap runs unless ci_method asks for one; when it does, the default is B = 10000 replications, and supplying seed makes the interval reproducible. Replications on which KR-20 cannot be computed are set aside and counted, among them a replication in which an item takes a single value, refused by name as the data would be: a resample leaves out a given respondent about 37 percent of the time (\((1 - 1/N)^N\), near \(e^{-1}\)), so an item passed by one respondent loses its variation in about a third of the resamples. The interval is computed from the replications that return a value; the counts travel in the bootstrap attribute described under reliability_alpha, print under the table, and are stated in a warning whenever a replication was set aside.

Comparison with other packages. The psych package computes the same quantity via alpha (since \(\alpha\) on 0/1 data is KR-20). reliability_kr20 restricts input to raw 0/1 data so the dichotomous-items assumption cannot be quietly violated, presents the historical formula in the documentation, and accompanies the point estimate with a confidence interval drawn from the methods compared in Kelley and Pornprasertmanit (2016).

References

Cronbach, L. J. (1951). Coefficient alpha and the internal structure of tests. Psychometrika, 16(3), 297–334.

Efron, B., & Tibshirani, R. J. (1993). An introduction to the bootstrap. New York, NY: Chapman & Hall/CRC.

Feldt, L. S. (1965). The approximate sampling distribution of Kuder-Richardson reliability coefficient twenty. Psychometrika, 30, 357–370.

Guttman, L. (1945). A basis for analyzing test-retest reliability. Psychometrika, 10(4), 255–282.

Kelley, K., & Cheng, Y. (2012). Estimation of and confidence interval formation for reliability coefficients of homogeneous measurement instruments. Methodology, 8, 39–50. doi:10.1027/1614-2241/a000036

Kelley, K., & Pornprasertmanit, S. (2016). Confidence intervals for population reliability coefficients: Evaluation of methods, recommendations, and software for composite measures. Psychological Methods, 21, 69–92. doi:10.1037/a0040086

Kuder, G. F., & Richardson, M. W. (1937). The theory of the estimation of test reliability. Psychometrika, 2, 151–160.

Maxwell, S. E., Delaney, H. D., & Kelley, K. (2027). Designing experiments and analyzing data: A model comparison perspective (4th ed.). Routledge.

Terry, L. J., & Kelley, K. (2012). Sample size planning for composite reliability coefficients: Accuracy in parameter estimation via narrow confidence intervals. British Journal of Mathematical and Statistical Psychology, 65, 371–401. doi:10.1111/j.2044-8317.2011.02030.x

Examples

set.seed(113)
# Ten dichotomous items with a single underlying ability.
N <- 300
J <- 10
ability <- rnorm(N)
loadings <- rep(0.6, J)
latent <- outer(ability, loadings) +
          matrix(rnorm(N * J, sd = sqrt(1 - 0.6^2)), N, J)
items <- (latent > 0) * 1
colnames(items) <- paste0("y", seq_len(J))

reliability_kr20(data = items)
#>  term       value
#>  estimate   0.774
#>  se         <NA> 
#>  ci_lower   0.734
#>  ci_upper   0.810
#>  conf_level 0.950
#>  N          300  
#>  N_complete 300  
#>  n_items    10   
reliability_kr20(data = items, ci_method = "bonett")
#>  term           value
#>  estimate       0.774
#>  se             0.020
#>  se_transformed 0.086
#>  ci_lower       0.732
#>  ci_upper       0.809
#>  conf_level     0.950
#>  N              300  
#>  N_complete     300  
#>  n_items        10   

# A bootstrap interval recomputes KR-20 on each of B resamples of the
# rows. B = 500 keeps the example quick; a reported interval deserves
# the default B = 10000, and seed makes the interval reproducible.
reliability_kr20(data = items, ci_method = "percentile", B = 500,
                 seed = 113)
#>  term       value
#>  estimate   0.774
#>  se         0.019
#>  ci_lower   0.739
#>  ci_upper   0.810
#>  conf_level 0.950
#>  N          300  
#>  N_complete 300  
#>  n_items    10   
#> 
#> Bootstrap: 500 replications attempted, 500 returned a value
